pos: n. (condition; standing; the settled circumstances of a man, a flock, a house or a land)
etymology: Latin status, from stare, to stand — the way a thing stands. In the Authorized Version state is never the modern political abstraction; it is the condition a person or people is actually in, and Scripture is always concerned that it be honestly known.
biblical_def: Two verses govern this word. First David's measure of a man: “Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity” (Psa 39:5). Not at his worst — at his best state, in the fullness of health, standing and success, a man is a breath. That is the honest reckoning from which all Christian ambition must begin. Second, Solomon's charge to the man responsible for others: “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds” (Pro 27:23). It is a farmer's proverb and has always been read as a pastor's and a father's. Oversight is not a title but an actual knowledge of the actual condition of those in one's charge, sheep by sheep. Proverbs adds the political form: “For the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof: but by a man of understanding and knowledge the state thereof shall be prolonged” (Pro 28:2). And our Lord gives the most sobering use: of the man swept and garnished from whom the unclean spirit went out and returned with seven worse, “the last state of that man is worse than the first” (Mat 12:45). Reformation without regeneration leaves a house empty and available.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines state as condition, the circumstances of a being or thing at any given time; and also rank, condition of life, and a political body.
webster_full: STATE, n. Condition; the circumstances of a being or thing at any given time.
1. Situation; condition; as, to be in a state of health or of sickness.
2. Rank; condition; quality; as the state of a nobleman.
3. Pomp; appearance of greatness; as, to be received in state.
4. A political body, or body politic; the whole body of people united under one government.
scriptures: Psa 39:5
Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity. Selah.
Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds.

Then goeth he, and taketh with himself seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter in and dwell there: and the last state of that man is worse than the first. Even so shall it be also unto this wicked generation.
Pro 28:2
For the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof: but by a man of understanding and knowledge the state thereof shall be prolonged.
corruption_summary: Moral improvement is offered where regeneration is needed; our Lord says the swept house ends in a worse state than it began.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 12:45 is the standing rebuke of every programme of reformation that stops short of the new birth. The house is swept and garnished — genuinely cleaner than it was, the obvious vice put out, the life visibly tidied — and it is empty. What returns is seven spirits worse than the first, and the last state of that man is worse than the first. Recovery programmes, moral crusades and behaviour-management discipleship can all produce a swept house. Only Christ can occupy it. This is precisely why the Reformed order puts regeneration first: a nature must be changed, not merely a conduct corrected.

The second thing to recover is Proverbs 27:23, which cuts against how oversight is now commonly exercised. Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks assumes a shepherd who can tell you, sheep by sheep, how each one is — and the verse goes on to say that riches are not for ever, and doth the crown endure to every generation? Position is temporary; knowledge of the flock is the work. An elder who knows the budget, the platform and the metrics but could not say which of his members is in trouble this month has the title without the office.
roots_summary: Hebrew matsab (H4673), a station, standing place; panim (H6440), face, condition; Greek eschatos (G2078), last — the last state.
roots_lines: Hebrew matsab (H4673) — a station, a post, a standing; Isaiah 22:19, from thy state shall he pull thee down.
Hebrew panim (H6440) — face, appearance, condition; Proverbs 27:23, the face of thy flocks — how they actually look.
Hebrew hebel (H1892) — vapour, breath, vanity; Psalm 39:5, every man at his best state.
Greek eschatos (G2078) — last, final; Matthew 12:45, Luke 11:26, the last state of that man.
Greek scholazo (G4980) — to be at leisure, to stand empty; Matthew 12:44, the house found empty, swept and garnished.
usage: “Every man at his best state is altogether vanity” — at his best.
“Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks” — sheep by sheep.
“The last state of that man is worse than the first” — a swept, empty house.

pos: n. pl. (business; the matters a man has in hand)
etymology: From the French à faire, to do — the things there are to do. In the Authorized Version the word covers a king's business, a province's administration, a good man's household management, and the concerns of a church for its imprisoned apostle.
biblical_def: “A good man sheweth favour, and lendeth: he will guide his affairs with discretion” (Psa 112:5). The psalm is an acrostic portrait of the man who feareth the LORD, and it includes his accounts. Generosity and prudence are set in one line: he lends, and he steers his business with judgment. Scripture never treats competence in ordinary matters as beneath piety. Daniel's three friends are set “over the affairs of the province of Babylon” (Dan 2:49) — and it is precisely their public competence that makes them visible when the image is set up: “There are certain Jews whom thou hast set over the affairs of the province of Babylon… these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods” (Dan 3:12). Faithfulness in office is what put them in the furnace. Paul uses the word for the traffic of love between churches: Tychicus is sent “that ye also may know my affairs, and how I do” (Eph 6:21), and he longs to hear of the Philippians' affairs, “that ye stand fast in one spirit” (Php 1:27). And to Timothy the soldier's rule: “No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier” (2Ti 2:4) — not that a minister may have no ordinary business, but that he may not be tangled in it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines affair as business of any kind, that which is done or is to be done; and in the plural, the transactions of a state or of private life.
webster_full: AFFAIR, n. Business of any kind; that which is done, or is to be done.
1. In the plural, transactions in general; as human affairs; political or ecclesiastical affairs.
2. Matters; concerns; as, to manage one's own affairs.
DISCRETION, n. Prudence, or knowledge and prudence; that discernment which enables a person to judge critically of what is correct and proper.
scriptures: A good man sheweth favour, and lendeth: he will guide his affairs with discretion.
No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.
Dan 3:12

There are certain Jews whom thou hast set over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego; these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
Eph 6:21
But that ye also may know my affairs, and how I do, Tychicus, a beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, shall make known to you all things:
corruption_summary: Spirituality is set against competence in ordinary business; Psalm 112 puts them in one line and Daniel's friends were faithful in both.
corruption_paragraphs: A persistent piety treats attention to money, planning and administration as worldly, and treats muddle as a mark of trusting God. Psalm 112 does not agree: the man who feareth the LORD, whose seed shall be mighty upon earth, guideth his affairs with discretion. Prudence in ordinary matters is a fruit of the fear of God, not a rival to it. Deacons were appointed precisely so that a church's business would be handled by men full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, which means the business was worth handling well.

The other side is 2 Timothy 2:4, and it is the discipline that keeps competence from becoming captivity. The soldier does not entangle himself — the picture is of a man caught in the ropes, unable to move when the order comes. Paul made tents; he was not entangled in tentmaking. Every believer, and especially every minister, has to weigh what he is holding by the question of whether he could let it go tomorrow if his Captain required it. Daniel's friends held high provincial office and walked away from all of it toward a furnace within a single afternoon.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar (H1697), a word, a matter, a thing; 'abidah (Aramaic H5673), work, administration; Greek pragmateia (G4230), business, affairs.
roots_lines: Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter, a thing done; 1 Chronicles 26:32, Psalm 112:5.
Aramaic 'abidah (H5673) — work, administration, service; Daniel 2:49, 3:12, the affairs of the province.
Greek pragmateia (G4230) — business, occupation, affair; 2 Timothy 2:4, the affairs of this life.
Greek empleko (G1707) — to entwine, to entangle; the soldier's danger — caught in ropes he cannot get free of.
Greek ta peri emou — the things concerning me; Ephesians 6:21, Philippians 1:27, Paul's idiom for news of himself.
usage: “He will guide his affairs with discretion” — in the psalm of the God-fearing man.
“Set over the affairs of the province of Babylon” — and reported for it.
“No man that warreth entangleth himself” — a soldier caught in ropes.

pos: n. (a condition or situation; a matter at law; in the phrase in any case, without exception)
etymology: Latin casus, a falling out, an occurrence — how a thing falls. The Authorized Version uses it both for a man's condition and for a legal matter, and the phrase in any case renders a Hebrew infinitive absolute meaning thou shalt surely do it.
biblical_def: “When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole?” (Joh 5:6). Thirty-eight years by the pool, and the Lord knew the length of it before He asked. The question is not cruel; it is the necessary question to a man who had built a life around a condition and had an explanation ready instead of an answer. Deuteronomy uses the word for the law's hard cases — “this is the case of the slayer, which shall flee thither, that he may live” (Deu 19:4), the manslayer who killed ignorantly and whom the cities of refuge existed to protect from the avenger. And twice the law uses in any case to close every loophole: the straying ox must be brought back — “thou shalt in any case bring them again unto thy brother” (Deu 22:1) — and the poor man's pledge must be returned by sundown, “that he may sleep in his own raiment, and bless thee: and it shall be righteousness unto thee before the LORD thy God” (Deu 24:13). Our Lord uses the same absolute form: “except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:20). And the psalmist ends the catalogue of national prosperity with the correction: “Happy is that people, that is in such a case: yea, happy is that people, whose God is the LORD” (Psa 144:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines case as literally that which falls or comes; hence a state of things, a condition; and in law, a cause or suit brought for decision.
webster_full: CASE, n. Literally, that which falls, comes or happens; an event.
1. State of things; condition; as, the case of the sick man is desperate.
2. In law, a cause or suit in court; a statement of facts for the opinion of counsel.
3. Contingency; a supposed event; as, in case of failure.
IN ANY CASE, at all events; certainly; without exception.
scriptures: John 5:6
When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole?
In any case thou shalt deliver him the pledge again when the sun goeth down, that he may sleep in his own raiment, and bless thee: and it shall be righteousness unto thee before the LORD thy God.
Mat 5:20
For I say unto you, That except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven.
Happy is that people, that is in such a case: yea, happy is that people, whose God is the LORD.
corruption_summary: Long affliction becomes an identity to be defended; our Lord asks a man of thirty-eight years whether he wills to be made whole.
corruption_paragraphs: John 5:6 asks a question the modern ear finds almost offensive, and it is worth sitting with rather than softening. Our Lord knew the man had been a long time in that case, and asked anyway: Wilt thou be made whole? The man's answer was not yes but an explanation of why it had never happened. Prolonged trouble can become the shape of a life — the way one is known, excused and understood — and healing then costs something. Nothing here mocks genuine affliction; the Lord healed him. But the question stands over every besetting condition that has quietly become a settled address.

The second recovery is the absolute in any case of the law. The straying ox goes back even if the brother is disliked; the poor man's coat goes back before sundown even though he still owes the money. The law refuses the exemptions we invent, and it attaches an unexpected promise: that he may sleep in his own raiment, and bless thee: and it shall be righteousness unto thee before the LORD thy God. The debtor sleeping warm is counted to the creditor as righteousness. Mercy in small transactions is treated by God as a serious moral act.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar (H1697), a matter; the infinitive absolute construction rendered in any case; Greek ou me (G3756, G3361), the emphatic double negative — in no case.
roots_lines: Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter, a case at law; Deuteronomy 19:4, the case of the slayer.
Hebrew infinitive absolute — the doubled verb (shob teshibem, returning thou shalt return them) rendered in any case; Deuteronomy 22:1, 24:13.
Hebrew 'abot (H5667) — a pledge, a pawn; the poor man's garment held for a debt.
Greek ou me (G3756 with G3361) — the emphatic double negative; Matthew 5:20, in no case enter into the kingdom.
Greek hugies (G5199) — whole, sound, healthy; John 5:6, wilt thou be made whole?
usage: “A long time in that case” — thirty-eight years, and He asked anyway.
“In any case thou shalt deliver him the pledge again” — before sundown.
“Happy is that people, whose God is the LORD” — the correction to the catalogue.

pos: n. (that which comes out; an outcome or issue — in Scripture, chiefly the one outcome that comes to all)
etymology: Latin evenire, to come out, to result. All three occurrences are in Ecclesiastes and all three are the same observation: under the sun, one event happeneth to them all.
biblical_def: “The wise man's eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness: and I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all” (Ecc 2:14). The Preacher grants without hesitation that wisdom excelleth folly as far as light excelleth darkness — and then observes that both men die. He presses it further: “All things come alike to all: there is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked; to the good and to the clean, and to the unclean; to him that sacrificeth, and to him that sacrificeth not” (Ecc 9:2), and calls it plainly an evil among all things done under the sun (Ecc 9:3). This is not scepticism and it is not despair; it is the honest report of what can be seen under the sun, which is the book's controlling phrase. Within the horizon of this life alone, the ledger does not balance, and Ecclesiastes refuses the pious lie that it does. The resolution is not offered by suppressing the observation but by lifting the horizon: the book ends with God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil. One event comes to all in this world. It is not the last event.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines event as that which comes, arrives or happens; an incident; and the consequence of an action, the issue or conclusion.
webster_full: EVENT, n. That which comes, arrives or happens; that which falls out; any incident good or bad.
1. The consequence of any thing; the issue; conclusion; end; that in which an action, operation or series of operations terminates.
EVENTUAL, a. Consequential; happening as a consequence or result.
scriptures: Ecc 2:14
The wise man's eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness: and I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all.
Ecc 9:2

All things come alike to all: there is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked; to the good and to the clean, and to the unclean; to him that sacrificeth, and to him that sacrificeth not: as is the good, so is the sinner; and he that sweareth, as he that feareth an oath.
Ecc 9:3

This is an evil among all things that are done under the sun, that there is one event unto all: yea, also the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
corruption_summary: Ecclesiastes is quoted as though it were the Bible's scepticism; it is the Bible's honesty about the world without its last chapter.
corruption_paragraphs: Two misuses of these verses are common. The unbelieving reading takes them as Scripture's own admission that life is meaningless and death ends all — a text quoted at funerals by men who never read the last two verses of the book. The pious misuse is the opposite: hurrying past the observation because it is uncomfortable, and insisting that in this life the righteous visibly prosper and the wicked visibly fall. Ecclesiastes was written against both. Its phrase under the sun is a deliberate limitation; it reports what an honest man sees from inside the world, and what he sees is that one event comes to the righteous and to the wicked alike.

The Christian answer is not a better observation but a further one. God shall bring every work into judgment (Ecc 12:14); the Preacher himself lifts the horizon at the close. And the New Testament names the event that broke the pattern: the resurrection of Christ, the firstfruits, after which death is no longer the one event but a defeated enemy. Psalm 73 walks the same road — Asaph envying the prosperity of the wicked until he went into the sanctuary of God, then understood I their end. The believer's comfort is not that the accounts balance now, but that the books are open and the day is fixed.
roots_summary: Hebrew miqreh (H4745), an occurrence, a chance, an event; tachath hashshemesh, under the sun; hebel (H1892), vapour, vanity.
roots_lines: Hebrew miqreh (H4745) — an accident, an occurrence, a lot that befalls; Ecclesiastes 2:14, 9:2-3 — the same word used of death in Ecclesiastes 3:19.
Hebrew tachath hashshemesh — under the sun; the book's controlling phrase, marking the limited horizon of its observation.
Hebrew hebel (H1892) — breath, vapour, vanity; the verdict on everything seen within that horizon.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment; Ecclesiastes 12:14, where the horizon is finally lifted.
Greek aparche (G536) — firstfruits; 1 Corinthians 15:20, Christ risen, the first of a harvest — the event that is not common to all.
usage: “One event happeneth to them all” — the wise man and the fool.
“There is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked” — under the sun.
“This is an evil among all things… that there is one event unto all”.

pos: n. (a view; the direction a thing looks — in the Authorized Version, the facing of the temple chambers and gates)
etymology: Latin prospicere, to look forward, from pro and specere, to look. In Ezekiel's temple vision the word does not mean expectation but orientation: which way a chamber or a gate looks.
biblical_def: In Ezekiel's temple the prospect of a room is its assignment. The chambers by the north gate, “whose prospect is toward the south, is for the priests, the keepers of the charge of the house” (Eze 40:45); and the chamber “whose prospect is toward the north is for the priests, the keepers of the charge of the altar: these are the sons of Zadok among the sons of Levi, which come near to the LORD to minister unto him” (Eze 40:46). Which way a man's chamber faced determined what he kept — the house or the altar — and the sons of Zadok, who had been faithful when the rest of the Levites went astray, are the ones who come near. Faithfulness in a former generation is honoured with nearness in this one. The measuring man then brings Ezekiel “forth toward the gate whose prospect is toward the east” (Eze 42:15) and measures it round about. And then the reason for all the measuring: “the glory of the LORD came into the house by the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east” (Eze 43:4). The glory that Ezekiel had watched depart from the city by the east in chapter eleven returns by the same gate. God comes back the way He left, and He comes into a house that has been measured and assigned down to the facing of its rooms.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prospect as view of things within the reach of the eye; and also the place and position of the front of a building, the direction it faces.
webster_full: PROSPECT, n. View of things within the reach of the eye.
1. View of things to come; view delineated by the mind; as the prospect of better times.
2. Place which affords an extended view.
3. Position of the front of a building; as a prospect toward the south or north.
scriptures: Eze 43:4
And the glory of the LORD came into the house by the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east.

And the chamber whose prospect is toward the north is for the priests, the keepers of the charge of the altar: these are the sons of Zadok among the sons of Levi, which come near to the LORD to minister unto him.
And he said unto me, This chamber, whose prospect is toward the south, is for the priests, the keepers of the charge of the house.
Now when he had made an end of measuring the inner house, he brought me forth toward the gate whose prospect is toward the east, and measured it round about.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The archaic sense — the direction a building faces — is simply unfamiliar to modern readers, who hear only the sense of expectation. No doctrine turns on the term.

The principle to recover is that God is exact about His house, and that the exactness is a mercy. Eight chapters of Ezekiel are given to measurements — gates, chambers, courts, the facing of every room — delivered to exiles who had watched the first temple burn. The vision does not begin with comfort; it begins with a measuring reed, and the comfort is in the measuring. A God who specifies which way a priest's chamber looks is a God who has not abandoned the project. And the vision ends with the glory returning by the east gate, the way it had gone out. What God removes in judgment He is able to bring back, by the same road.
roots_summary: Hebrew panim (H6440), face — the face or facing of a chamber; derek (H1870), way; kabod (H3519), glory.
roots_lines: Hebrew panim (H6440) — face, front; in Ezekiel 40-43 the face of a chamber or gate, rendered prospect.
Hebrew derek (H1870) — way, road, direction; the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east.
Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, weight; Ezekiel 43:4, the glory of the LORD returning to the house.
Hebrew Tsadoq (H6659) — Zadok, righteous; the priestly line kept near because it kept the charge.
Hebrew mishmereth (H4931) — a charge, a watch, a duty kept; what each chamber's occupants were responsible for.
usage: “By the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east” — the glory came back.
“Whose prospect is toward the north is for the priests… of the altar”.
“He brought me forth toward the gate… and measured it round about”.

pos: adj. (the older form of situated: placed, seated in a particular position)
etymology: Latin situs, position. The seventeenth-century adjective drops the modern -ed. Two of its three occurrences describe cities whose position was their pride and, in the event, their false confidence.
biblical_def: “Say unto Tyrus, O thou that art situate at the entry of the sea, which art a merchant of the people for many isles… O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty” (Eze 27:3). The city's position — an island fortress at the sea's entry, the trading hub of the Mediterranean — was the foundation of both her wealth and her self-estimate. Ezekiel spends a chapter listing her merchandise and then sinks her: thy riches, and thy fairs… shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin. Nahum uses the word to make the same argument to Nineveh, by pointing to a city that had already fallen: “Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?” (Nah 3:8). Thebes had every natural defence and was carried away captive; the argument is that Nineveh's walls are no better. The third occurrence is a plain topographical note in the passage where Jonathan and his armourbearer climb between two rocks: “The forefront of the one was situate northward over against Michmash” (1Sa 14:5) — and two men went up against a garrison, because there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives situate as placed with respect to any other object; and situation as position, seat, location in respect to something else.
webster_full: SITUATE, a. Placed with respect to any other object; as a town situated on a hill.
1. Placed; consisting.
SITUATION, n. Position; seat; location in respect to something else.
1. State; condition; as, a happy or an unhappy situation.
scriptures: Eze 27:3
And say unto Tyrus, O thou that art situate at the entry of the sea, which art a merchant of the people for many isles, Thus saith the Lord GOD; O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty.
Nah 3:8
Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?
The forefront of the one was situate northward over against Michmash, and the other southward over against Gibeah.
corruption_summary: Advantages of position are trusted as security; God asks Nineveh whether she is better than a city with better walls that fell.
corruption_paragraphs: Nahum 3:8 is the whole argument against trusting circumstances. Art thou better than populous No? — a city with rivers round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and she went into captivity, her young children dashed at the top of all the streets. Nineveh was being invited to look at a fortress stronger than her own and draw the obvious conclusion. Every generation has its own version of the impregnable position: an economy, an institution, a family standing, a church's history. Scripture's consistent answer is that the position is real and the security is imaginary. Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.

Tyre adds the interior version of the same sin: thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty. The city's position produced a self-estimate, and the self-estimate is what Ezekiel indicts. Advantages that come by God's providence — a good location, an inherited business, natural gifts — are received and then quietly reclassified as merit. The corrective is Paul's question, which is unanswerable and therefore usually left unasked: what hast thou that thou didst not receive?
roots_summary: Hebrew yashab (H3427), to sit, to dwell, to be seated; mabo' yam, the entry of the sea; No' (H4996), Thebes.
roots_lines: Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to sit, remain, dwell; Ezekiel 27:3, Nahum 3:8 — the city sits where it is.
Hebrew mabo' (H3996) — entrance, entry; Ezekiel 27:3, the entry of the sea.
Hebrew No' (H4996) — No, the Egyptian Thebes; Nahum 3:8, Jeremiah 46:25, Ezekiel 30:14-16.
Hebrew chel (H2426) — a rampart, an outer wall; Thebes' defence, and the sea itself.
Hebrew klilath yophi — perfect of beauty; Ezekiel 27:3, Tyre's own verdict on herself — a phrase Lamentations 2:15 applies to Jerusalem.
usage: “O thou that art situate at the entry of the sea” — and she said, I am of perfect beauty.
“Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers?”
“Situate northward over against Michmash” — and two men went up.

pos: v. (came after and took the place of; in the Authorized Version, dispossessed and inherited — never “prospered”)
etymology: Latin succedere, to go under or come after. The modern sense of prospering is absent from the Authorized Version; all three occurrences mean to take another people's place in their land, and the Hebrew is literally inherited.
biblical_def: All three occurrences stand in one passage of Deuteronomy, where Moses is explaining why Israel must not attack Edom, Moab or Ammon. “The Horims also dwelt in Seir beforetime; but the children of Esau succeeded them, when they had destroyed them from before them, and dwelt in their stead; as Israel did unto the land of his possession, which the LORD gave unto them” (Deu 2:12). And of the Ammonites and the giants before them: “A people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims; but the LORD destroyed them before them; and they succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead” (Deu 2:21). The point Moses is making is startling. God had given Seir to Esau and Ar to the children of Lot, and had cleared out the previous inhabitants for them, exactly as He was about to do for Israel in Canaan. Israel therefore may not touch a foot of it. The God of Israel is not a tribal deity who manages only His own people's conquests; He assigns lands to nations who do not know Him — the doctrine Paul preached at Athens, that God hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation. Israel's title to Canaan was a gift, and so was Edom's to Seir, and the same Giver protected both.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines succeed as to follow in order, to take the place which another has left; and notes the sense of obtaining the object desired as a distinct use.
webster_full: SUCCEED, v.t. To follow in order; to take the place which another has left.
1. To follow; to come after; to be subsequent or consequent.
2. To prosper; to obtain the object desired; to accomplish what is attempted or intended.
SUCCESSION, n. A following of things in order; a series of persons or things following one another in time or place.
scriptures: Deu 2:12

The Horims also dwelt in Seir beforetime; but the children of Esau succeeded them, when they had destroyed them from before them, and dwelt in their stead; as Israel did unto the land of his possession, which the LORD gave unto them.
Deu 2:21
A people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims; but the LORD destroyed them before them; and they succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead:
Deu 2:22
As he did to the children of Esau, which dwelt in Seir, when he destroyed the Horims from before them; and they succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead even unto this day:
corruption_summary: Success is read into a word that means dispossession; and God's rule over the nations is shrunk to His rule over the church.
corruption_paragraphs: The English word has drifted so far that a reader meets succeeded in Deuteronomy 2 and hears achievement, where Moses means that one people took another people's land. That drift matters beyond the lexicon, because it is a small instance of how the vocabulary of success has colonized Christian speech generally — successful ministries, successful marriages, a successful life — importing a measure Scripture does not use. The Bible's categories are faithful and unfaithful, fruitful and barren, wise and foolish. Joseph in prison was not successful; he was blessed, which is a different word and a different scale.

The doctrine in the passage is worth as much as the lexicography. God assigned Seir to Esau and Ar to Lot's children, dispossessed nations to make room for them, and forbade Israel to take an inch of it. He governs the nations that do not worship Him as truly as the nation that does — the Most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. Israel had no ground for supposing her title was superior in kind to Edom's; both were gifts, and the Giver defended both. That is a sharp word to any people inclined to read its own borders as a divine endorsement.
roots_summary: Hebrew yarash (H3423), to take possession, to dispossess, to inherit; tachath (H8478), in the place of, instead of; gebul (H1366), border.
roots_lines: Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to seize, possess, dispossess, inherit; the verb rendered succeeded in Deuteronomy 2:12, 2:21-22, and everywhere else possess or drive out.
Hebrew tachath (H8478) — under, in place of, instead of; dwelt in their stead.
Hebrew Chori (H2752) — the Horims (Horites), the cave-dwellers of Seir before Edom.
Hebrew 'Anaqim (H6062) — the Anakims, the tall people whose report terrified the spies in Numbers 13.
Greek horothesia (G3734) — the fixing of boundaries; Acts 17:26, God determined the bounds of their habitation.
usage: “The children of Esau succeeded them… and dwelt in their stead”.
“The LORD destroyed them before them; and they succeeded them” — for Ammon.
“As he did to the children of Esau” — the reason Israel must not touch Seir.

pos: v. (sent away; released from attendance or duty)
etymology: Latin dimittere, to send away. Three occurrences, and each concerns the orderly ending of a gathering — the courses of the priests, the messengers of a council, and a riot.
biblical_def: Two of the three are about the orderly close of a lawful assembly, and one is about the closing of an unlawful one. When Jehoiada put Joash on the throne and executed Athaliah, the priest kept the temple rota running through the crisis: “for Jehoiada the priest dismissed not the courses” (2Ch 23:8) — both the incoming and the outgoing shifts were kept on duty. In a moment when everything was at stake he did not suspend the ordinary order of God's house; he doubled it. After the Jerusalem council settled the question of the Gentiles, “when they were dismissed, they came to Antioch: and when they had gathered the multitude together, they delivered the epistle” (Act 15:30) — the delegates were formally sent, and formally received, and the letter was read to the whole congregation. Church decisions in Acts are made and communicated in the open. And the third: the riot at Ephesus, where the townclerk quieted a two-hour mob with a plain appeal to lawful process — the law is open, there are deputies, let them implead one another — and “when he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly” (Act 19:41). A pagan magistrate defending due process against a religious mob protected the church that day, which is a use of the civil sword Paul would defend in Romans 13.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dismiss as to send away, to permit to depart; to discard, to remove from office or employment.
webster_full: DISMISS, v.t. To send away; properly, to give leave of departure; to permit to depart.
1. To discard; to remove from office, service or employment.
2. To send or remove from a docket; to discontinue; as, to dismiss a bill in chancery.
DISMISSED, pp. Sent away; permitted to depart; removed from office or employment.
scriptures: So the Levites and all Judah did according to all things that Jehoiada the priest had commanded, and took every man his men that were to come in on the sabbath, with them that were to go out on the sabbath: for Jehoiada the priest dismissed not the courses.
So when they were dismissed, they came to Antioch: and when they had gathered the multitude together, they delivered the epistle:
And when he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The verb is ordinary and its biblical uses are procedural.

The principle to recover is that God's work is done decently and in order, especially in a crisis. Jehoiada was overthrowing a usurping queen and did not dismiss the courses; the temple service ran through the coup. The Jerusalem council did not leave its decision to rumour but sent named men with a letter to be read aloud to the gathered church. And the Ephesian townclerk quieted a mob by pointing to courts, deputies and lawful assemblies. Order is not the enemy of zeal in Scripture; it is the ordinary channel through which zeal is kept from becoming a riot. Paul draws the rule from the character of God Himself: God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
roots_summary: Hebrew patar (H6362), to let go, release; Greek apoluo (G630), to release, to send away; ekklesia (G1577), an assembly called out.
roots_lines: Hebrew patar (H6362) — to set free, let go, dismiss; 2 Chronicles 23:8.
Hebrew machleqoth (H4256) — divisions, courses; the priestly rota David had organized, kept running through the coup.
Greek apoluo (G630) — to loose from, to send away, to dismiss; Acts 15:30, 19:41.
Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly, a called-out gathering; Acts 19:41 uses it of the civic assembly at Ephesus — the ordinary Greek sense behind the word for the church.
Greek grammateus (G1122) — a scribe, here the town clerk of Ephesus, the city's chief civil officer.
usage: “Jehoiada the priest dismissed not the courses” — in the middle of a coup.
“When they were dismissed, they came to Antioch” — and read the letter aloud.
“He dismissed the assembly” — a magistrate against a mob.

pos: v. (raised to rank or honour; promoted)
etymology: Old French avancer, to move forward, from Latin ab ante. In the Authorized Version the verb is always about being lifted into place by somebody else — and Scripture is careful about who does the lifting.
biblical_def: Samuel puts the doctrine in one sentence at the end of his public ministry: “It is the LORD that advanced Moses and Aaron, and that brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt” (1Sa 12:6). The two greatest men in Israel's history were not self-made; they were advanced, and by the same hand that brought the nation out. Against that stands the book of Esther, which uses the word three times and makes it the hinge of the plot. “King Ahasuerus promote[d] Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes” (Est 3:1). Haman then recites his own promotion to his friends: “all the things wherein the king had promoted him, and how he had advanced him above the princes and servants of the king” (Est 5:11) — and adds that all this availeth him nothing so long as Mordecai sits at the gate. A man advanced above every prince in the empire was made miserable by one man who would not bow. And the book closes with the reversal: “the declaration of the greatness of Mordecai, whereunto the king advanced him” (Est 10:2). The same verb, the same king, the opposite man. God's name never appears in Esther, and His hand is on every page.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines advance as to raise to a higher rank, to promote; to forward, to accelerate growth; and advanced as promoted, raised to a higher rank.
webster_full: ADVANCE, v.t. To bring forward; to move further in front.
1. To promote; to raise to a higher rank; as, to advance one to the rank of a general.
2. To improve or make better, which is considered as a moving forward.
ADVANCED, pp. Moved forward; promoted; improved; furnished beforehand.
PROMOTION, n. Advancement in place or in honor; exaltation in rank.
scriptures: And Samuel said unto the people, It is the LORD that advanced Moses and Aaron, and that brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt.
Est 5:11

And Haman told them of the glory of his riches, and the multitude of his children, and all the things wherein the king had promoted him, and how he had advanced him above the princes and servants of the king.
Est 3:1
After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him.
Est 10:2

And all the acts of his power and of his might, and the declaration of the greatness of Mordecai, whereunto the king advanced him, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?
corruption_summary: Advancement is pursued as the reward of merit; Scripture says promotion cometh neither from the east nor from the west, and shows Haman miserable at the top.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning account of advancement is meritocratic: a man rises because he is worth it, and if he does not rise he is not. Psalm 75:6-7 denies the premise flatly — promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south. But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another. Samuel says the same of Moses and Aaron. This is not an argument against diligence, which Proverbs commends everywhere, nor a promise that the diligent will always be raised. It relocates the decision. A believer works faithfully in his calling and leaves the setting up and the putting down where it belongs.

Haman is the case study, and his misery is the part usually skipped. He was advanced above all the princes of a world empire, had riches, ten children and a private invitation to the queen's banquet — and he said, yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate. Envy is not cured by elevation; it follows a man up. He went home and built a gallows fifty cubits high, and was hanged on it. The Christian answer is not a better position but a mortified heart, and the discipline for it is the one Paul learned: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'asah (H6213), to make — the LORD who made Moses and Aaron; gadal (H1431), to make great; nasa' (H5375), to lift up.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'asah (H6213) — to do, to make; 1 Samuel 12:6, the LORD that made Moses and Aaron — the margin's reading, and the sense of advancement.
Hebrew gadal (H1431) — to make great, to magnify; Esther 3:1, 5:11, 10:2 — the same verb for Haman's rise and Mordecai's.
Hebrew nasa' (H5375) — to lift, to raise, to bear; Esther 3:1, the king lifted him above all the princes.
Hebrew Agagi (H91) — Agagite; Haman's descent from Agag the Amalekite king Saul spared — an old disobedience returning centuries later.
Greek hupsoo (G5312) — to lift up, to exalt; Luke 14:11, whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.
usage: “It is the LORD that advanced Moses and Aaron”.
“How he had advanced him above the princes” — and it availed him nothing.
“The greatness of Mordecai, whereunto the king advanced him” — the same verb, reversed.

pos: n. and v. (the head; hence to number by heads, and to cut the hair of the head)
etymology: From an old Germanic word for the head or top — the same root that gives polled cattle and, much later, a poll of voters counted by heads. In the Authorized Version the word means the head itself, and both its senses follow from that.
biblical_def: The old English poll is the head, and Scripture uses it in both directions. Counted: “Thou shalt even take five shekels apiece by the poll, after the shekel of the sanctuary shalt thou take them” (Num 3:47) — the redemption money for the firstborn of Israel who exceeded the number of the Levites, five shekels a head. A census in Israel is a counting of heads for a redemption price, which is why David's numbering without the ransom brought a plague. Cut: the priests of Ezekiel's temple “shall not shave their heads, nor suffer their locks to grow long; they shall only poll their heads” (Eze 44:20) — neither the shaven head of pagan mourning nor the long unbound hair of the Nazarite, but trimmed. The priesthood was to look like neither the mourner nor the ascetic; a settled, ordinary appearance was itself a testimony. And Micah, ordering a nation into mourning: “Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children; enlarge thy baldness as the eagle; for they are gone into captivity from thee” (Mic 1:16). The delicate children — the ones raised carefully, in comfort — are the ones carried away, and the prophet tells the mothers to cut off their hair.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines poll as the head of a person, and hence a register of heads or persons; and as a verb, to lop the tops of trees or to cut off the hair of the head.
webster_full: POLL, n. The head of a person, or the back part of the head.
1. A register of heads, that is, of persons; as, to take the poll.
2. An election, or the place where an election is held; so called from the counting of heads.
POLL, v.t. To lop the tops of trees; to clip; to shear; as, to poll the head.
1. To enter or register the names of persons.
scriptures: Num 3:47
Thou shalt even take five shekels apiece by the poll, after the shekel of the sanctuary shalt thou take them: (the shekel is twenty gerahs:)
Neither shall they shave their heads, nor suffer their locks to grow long; they shall only poll their heads.
Mic 1:16
Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children; enlarge thy baldness as the eagle; for they are gone into captivity from thee.
corruption_summary: Ministers are shaped by the extremes of the surrounding culture; Ezekiel forbids the priests both the shaven head and the flowing locks.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 44:20 is a small verse with a durable application. The priest was to look like neither of the two available religious types: not the shaven head of the pagan mourning rites Israel was forbidden to copy, and not the long unbound hair that marked the Nazarite's temporary separation. He was to be trimmed — ordinary, kept, unremarkable. The temptation for those who serve God has always been to signal by appearance, whether by adopting the surrounding culture's markers or by adopting a conspicuous holiness that advertises itself. The ceremonial detail is fulfilled and no longer binds; the instinct behind it — that a minister's appearance should draw no attention to itself in either direction — has not aged.

Micah supplies the other application, and it is severe. Poll thee for thy delicate children — the children reared in comfort and carefully spared every hardship are the ones described going into captivity. A generation raised for softness has no defence when the Assyrian comes. Scripture's alternative is not harshness toward children, which it forbids, but the deliberate formation of them in the fear of the LORD — teaching them diligently, sitting, walking, lying down and rising up — so that they are ready for a world that will not be delicate with them.
roots_summary: Hebrew gulgoleth (H1538), a skull, a head — and the root of Golgotha; kasam (H3697), to trim or shear; qarach (H7139), to make bald.
roots_lines: Hebrew gulgoleth (H1538) — a skull, a head, a poll; Numbers 3:47, Exodus 38:26 — and the Aramaic form gives Golgotha, the place of a skull.
Hebrew kasam (H3697) — to shear, to trim; Ezekiel 44:20, they shall only poll their heads — its only occurrence.
Hebrew qarach (H7139) — to make bald; Micah 1:16, a sign of mourning forbidden to priests but commanded here to a nation.
Hebrew pidyom (H6306) — a ransom, redemption money; the five shekels a head for the firstborn.
Hebrew 'anugim (H8588) — delicate, dainty, tenderly reared; Micah 1:16, the children carried away.
usage: “Five shekels apiece by the poll” — redemption money, head by head.
“They shall only poll their heads” — neither shaven nor flowing.
“Poll thee for thy delicate children” — and they were the ones taken.
